newsitem.title: Bosnia: Explosives threat to Pope in Sarajevo.
newsitem.headline: Explosives threat to Pope in Sarajevo.

text.p: Police averted a potential attempt to assassinate Pope John Paul during his visit to Sarajevo on Saturday when they disarmed 23 landmines found under a bridge on the road from the airport into the Bosnian capital.
The Pope left Rome to carry out his 25-hour visit despite the heightened concerns for his safety.
U.N. police spokesman Alexander Ivanko said 23 mines coonnected to a detonator and a remote control device were found on Saturday morning.
Roman Catholic Church authorities refused to confirm that the papal motorcade planned to cross the bridge but it would be the usual route into the city.
"It seems a worker saw a person in that area this morning and advised the police," Ivanko, spokesman for the United Nations mission, told Reuters.
"On arrival the Bosnian police and the International Police Task Force found 23 mines connected to a detonator with additional plastic explosives and a remote control," Ivanko said.
Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation bomb experts believed the explosives were "freshly planted", he added.
Bosnian authorities and international police officers met to review the security situation after the mines were found.
A spokesman for the Roman Catholic archdiocese in Sarajevo said the Pope's trip was going ahead despite the discovery of the explosives.
"Nobody is speaking about cancelling the visit," said spokesman Ivo Tomasevic.
Earlier, a Bosnian police officer said: "We inspected the bridge yesterday and there was nothing there."
Large numbers of policemen have been posted along the boulevard which leads to the city centre. During the 1992-95 Bosnian war, city residents used to queue at a pipe under the bridge to fetch water.
A series of bomb attacks on Roman Catholic churches and Islamic mosques in the past two months had raised concerns for the Pope's safety during his historic two-day visit.
Bosnian police, supported by the NATO-led peace force, announced elaborate security precautions this week, deploying bomb disposal and anti-sniper teams.
The Pope was forced to cancel a scheduled visit in September 1994, while the war was still raging, after Bosnian Serb forces laying siege to the city refused to give security guarantees.
The Serb member of the new collective presidency, Momcilo Krajisnik, supported the invitation for this week's Papal trip.
The Vatican said the 76-year-old Pontiff would call for reconciliation and forgiveness among Bosnia's Moslems, Catholic Croats and Orthodox Serbs.
